summary: Old Bodija remains one of Ibadan's most prestigious, leafy, and central residential enclaves, favored by civil servants, expatriates, and upper-middle-class families. While it boasts mature greenery, generous plot sizes, and peaceful streets, many properties are older builds undergoing modernization, sitting right beside increasingly commercialized avenues.
powerExpectations: Old Bodija mostly runs on IBEDC Band A and Band B feeders, particularly those tied to the Secretariat and University of Ibadan grid lines, delivering an average of 14 to 20 hours daily. However, transformer tripping occurs during heavy downpours, so a minimum 2.5kVA inverter system or petrol generator remains non-negotiable for seamless remote work.
waterAndDrainage: Sitting on a relatively elevated plateau, Old Bodija escapes the catastrophic flash flooding seen along the Eleyele or Odo-Ona basins, though poor roadside drainage on peripheral streets can cause localized ponding. Almost all houses rely on motorized boreholes (typically 40 to 60 meters deep); ensure your prospective compound has a functional filtration unit, as proximity to decades-old soakaways can affect groundwater purity.
securityAndNightMovement: Most streets operate strict Community Development Association (CDA) gating policies, with inner gates locking firmly between 10:00 PM and 11:00 PM and requiring night guard clearance thereafter. Monthly vigilante/estate security dues run between ₦5,000 and ₦15,000, and police presence is solid due to the nearby Bodija Police Station and VIP residences.
transportationAndCommute: Commuting is arguably the best in Ibadan: Dugbe is 15 minutes away, and the State Secretariat is under 7 minutes. Micra cabs are plentiful along Osuntokun Avenue and the UI–Secretariat axis, while Bolt and inDrive cabs arrive within 3 to 5 minutes anywhere in the neighborhood. Okada bikes are restricted from entering certain private closes.
localHotspots: Bodija Market (periphery for wholesale fresh food)
tenantTips: Differentiate between purely residential streets and commercial corridors like Osuntokun Avenue to avoid living next to lounges or event centers with night-long noise pollution.
Carefully inspect plumbing and electrical conduits in remodeled 1970s/1980s colonial houses; landlords often apply fresh paint over obsolete, brittle pipes and wiring.
Ask the street's CDA executive or neighbors directly about pending transformer development levies before paying the landlord, as new tenants are frequently blindsided with historical debt.
Confirm the exact water pumping schedule if moving into a multi-tenant apartment block, as shared borehole management often sparks friction.
